title: Senior's toolkit: bytes, encodings and randomness
summary: The commands and .NET APIs you use to look at raw bytes, convert hex and Base64, and make secrets that cannot be guessed.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: bytes, encodings and randomness
steps.body: Every crypto bug report starts with someone pasting bytes: a key, a token, a hash. These are the tools experienced engineers use to see what those bytes really are, and to make new secrets safely.

toolkit.what: Hex dump of a file or of stdin. Shows the real bytes: a BOM, a stray newline at the end of a key, a file that is Base64 text rather than binary.
flags: plain hex, no offsets or ASCII column
reverse: turn plain hex back into bytes
toolkit.when: a key or signature "should match" and does not

toolkit.what: Encode or decode Base64 on the command line. It knows only standard Base64 (`+` and `/`), not the URL-safe alphabet JWTs use.
flags: (GNU) do not wrap the output at 76 characters

toolkit.what: Bytes from a cryptographically secure generator. The quickest way to make a key, a webhook secret or a test token.
flags: write raw bytes to a file

toolkit.what: Bytes to hex and back, and to Base64 and back, in .NET. `ToHexStringLower` (.NET 9) matches what `sha256sum` and `openssl` print.
flags: hex to bytes; accepts upper or lower case

toolkit.what: URL-safe Base64 (`-` and `_`, no padding) from `System.Buffers.Text` (.NET 9). It is what JWTs, PKCE and most tokens in URLs use.
flags: back to a `byte[]`; padding is optional

toolkit.what: The secure random generator in .NET. Never use `System.Random` for anything an attacker must not guess.
flags: a new array of 32 random bytes (a 256-bit key)
an unbiased random number in a range, e.g. a 6-digit code
a random hex string of 32 characters (.NET 8)
a random string drawn from your own alphabet (.NET 8)

toolkit.what: Text to bytes. Crypto works on bytes, so both sides must agree on UTF-8, or the same string gives different hashes.
flags: bytes back to text (only for bytes that really are text)
a UTF-8 byte literal, no runtime conversion

steps.explain: Base64url swaps `+` for `-` and `/` for `_`, and .NET's `Base64Url` leaves out the `=` padding. `H`, `i` and `!` are bytes 0x48, 0x69 and 0x21.

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
pairs: turns plain hex back into bytes
makes a 256-bit secret as 64 hex characters

steps.prompt: A partner sends a webhook secret: `q7-Lm_x0Zk2WcA`. You try to decode it and get an error. What is going on?
options: It is Base64url (it contains `-` and `_`); decode it with `Base64Url.DecodeFromChars` or translate `-_` to `+/` and add padding first
The secret is corrupt; ask the partner for a new one
`base64 -d` cannot decode secrets shorter than 16 characters
steps.explain: Standard Base64 never contains `-` or `_`. Those two characters (and missing `=` padding) are the tell for Base64url, which `base64 -d` and `Convert.FromBase64String` both reject.

steps.prompt: Make a 256-bit encryption key and a 32-character hex token for a password-reset link.
steps.explain: `GetBytes(32)` returns 32 secure random bytes. `GetHexString(32, lowercase: true)` returns 32 hex characters (16 random bytes). `NextBytes` belongs to `System.Random`, which is predictable.

items: A SHA-256 digest in a log line people compare by eye
The body of a PEM file
A binary value inside a JSON config, compactly
The three parts of a JWT
A random token in a URL query string

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When two systems disagree about a key or a hash, dump both sides with `xxd` before you read any code: a trailing newline or the wrong Base64 alphabet explains most of them. Make every secret with `openssl rand` or `RandomNumberGenerator`, never by typing one or by `System.Random`.
